1d3840e69c8069d7.title: Two Kinds of Failure and How to Respond to Both
1d3840e69c8069d7.summary:
In this episode, Jamie and Donna Winship talk about the difference between failing at something and becoming a failure. Drawing from a study on high-resiliency people (including Navy SEALs), they show how resilient people treat unmet expectations as data and opportunity rather than identity.They distinguish two kinds of “failure”: outcomes that didn’t go as expected (like Elijah when the brook dried up) and moral failure or sin (like David). In both cases, the biblical response is the same—truth-telling, fixing your eyes on Jesus, and moving forward. Forgiveness is already present (Ephesians and Colossians); confession aligns us with what Christ has already done. Using the story of the man at the pool of Bethesda, they show how Jesus redirects our gaze from the problem to Himself so we can pick up our mat and walk.Whether you’re carrying shame from a moral failure or stuck because something didn’t work out, the invitation is the same: stop sitting in the failure, receive what’s already yours, and keep going with joy.

But there’s an important distinction between being thankful and being grateful. Thankfulness is often directed at a person or a circumstance. Gratitude goes deeper. It is not based on anything fragile or fading, but is secured in the finished work of Christ and your oneness with Him.In this conversation they explore:

The difference between thankful and grateful (and why it matters)
How to soak your requests in gratitude so anxiety doesn’t distract you (Philippians 4)

What it means to live overwhelmed by God’s opinion of you
The powerful Corrie ten Boom story of the flea-infested barracks
A simple daily practice: hand over your heart, naming five unchanging, unfading things you’re grateful for.

Your purpose has already been concluded in Christ. From that place of redeemed innocence and security, true thankfulness flows naturally—no matter what the day holds.

c38319e5cb5d234d.title: Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin
c38319e5cb5d234d.summary:
By Mark Ellis —

Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego.

As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, especially with the Rigs-to-Reefs program, when oil drilling platforms are decommissioned. “We work with the oil companies to repurpose certain parts of the platform, retrofit it so that it can remain in place and continue to function as an artificial reef,” she told God Reports.

Amber’s work has taken her around the world, with many dive experiences and encounters in the ocean with marine life.

But there is one story she will never forget.

It happened in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after Amber graduated from Scripps Institute and was invited on a research industry cruise with oil company representatives, scientists, and regulators on a liveaboard vessel.

At the Flower Garden National Banks, a marine protected area 200 miles offshore, Amber was excited about her first dive, but slightly nervous. “You don’t know what you’re going to see or what this experience is going to be like,” she recalls.

Each diver had to jump off the vessel to get in the water. “We’re all geared up with our snorkel, our buoyancy control device, our wetsuit, and fins are the last thing you put on. So, I put on my fins and I jumped off the side of the boat.”

“The second that I hit the water, one of my fins fell off, and I looked down and watched as it slowly descended to the bottom.”

Amber glanced over at her dive buddy, and said, “I’m gonna go down. I’m going down.”

Normally she would wait for her dive partner and they would go down together, but in this case, she thought, “I can’t (wait). I gotta go get my fin.”

So Amber slowly began to descend to the bottom, about 60 feet below the ocean surface. “I felt completely lost. I was in a completely new area. I never dove before, and now I only had one fin.”

She realized there were major currents that could have moved her fin in any direction. “I realized I can’t really swim with just one fin. So now not only am I at depth, but I’m handicapped with just one fin, and I started to feel pretty nervous.”

It would probably take her 10 minutes to get back the surface, with safety stops. At the moment before panic set in, she looked upward and saw an amazing sight.

It was a giant manta ray, with wings extending at least 10 feet. “Its wingspan was double mine. Its arms were out, and it was coming up over the side of a reef.

“I’ve never seen a manta ray like this before. It totally took my breath away, it was so magnificent.”

She noted that manta rays are known in the ocean community to be “majestic, God-connected creatures with an understanding maybe beyond what humans can fully comprehend. They see the world and feel it in another way,” she notes.

Mantas have the largest known brain of any fish. Their brains are large in absolute terms and relative to body size, which is also true of elephants, dolphins, and people. Their brains have enlarged areas associated with intelligence, vision, and motor coordination, and some of their brain cells are more like those in birds and mammals than in other fish.(1)

As the manta ray drew close to Amber, she had an unusual communication experience.

“I felt this sense where it said, ‘I want you to follow me. I’m going to help you find your fin.’

Amber’s diving partner had just descended next to her, and they both began to swim after the manta. “I was barely making it, following this manta ray across the reef. At this point, I was so excited to see a manta ray. I kind of forgot about being handicapped, and I was just trying to go as fast as I can to keep up with it.

Then Amber got the surprise of her life. “All of a sudden, I looked down, and it had taken us to where my fin had landed.”

She says it was like finding a needle in a haystack.  You might think that your fin would just sink to the bottom, but with all the currents and everything happening, it really could have gone anywhere. And I felt so fortunate, and I do feel like God connected into that manta ray and helped guide me back to my fin, and I put the fin on.

Then the manta ray disappeared, not to be seen again.

“I remember feeling so grateful, so moved by that experience. And I have two young children who often ask me for stories around bedtime, and I started telling it to them because it was a story of how God is watching out for us in ways that we might not expect, when you might feel like you’re at the last moment of hope.”

  1. Jessica Knoth, “Manta Rays – They’re Just Like Us,” Currents: A Student Blog, School of Marine and Environmental Affairs, University of Washington, March 28, 2018, https://smea.uw.edu/currents/manta-rays-theyre-just-like-us/.

099938282e9f6fdf.title: Houston’s Epiphanies: Turrell and Rothko
099938282e9f6fdf.summary:
The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art.

Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation.

Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program.

The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them.

For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention.

From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel.

Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name.

Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies.

There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence.

Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. One is animated by the changing light of the sky, the other by the stillness of darkened canvases. Yet both offer something increasingly rare in contemporary life: an invitation to stop, observe, and reflect.

And perhaps that is their shared epiphany.

Amid two artistic landmarks dedicated to thought, reflection, and deep contemplation, I was reminded that beauty can provide solace even when it cannot resolve life’s deepest questions. Beauty does not eliminate suffering, nor does it necessarily explain tragedy. But it can create a space in which suffering is acknowledged, mystery is embraced, and hope is allowed to emerge. Beauty is not merely decorative or incidental to human experience. It is fundamental to how we perceive and engage with the world.

As a Christian, I understand beauty as a reflection of the Creator, whose handiwork is evident in both the grandeur of creation and the creative capacities of those made in his image. Even when beauty emerges from brokenness, it can remind us that suffering does not have the final word.

Leaving Houston’s two remarkable sanctuaries, I carried with me more than memories of light and color. I carried a renewed conviction that beauty is not simply something we observe; it is something through which we encounter the mystery and meaning of existence.

673b8898e1b8e02c.title: Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success
673b8898e1b8e02c.summary:
While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.”

From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity, Faith Founded on Fact, and The Shape of the Past, helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry.

Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work.

The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions.

From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith.

The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth.

The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions.

The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning.

On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton.

Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty.

As I reflected on the weekend, I was reminded of the Festschrift Christianity for the Tough-Minded, a collection of scholarly essays honoring Montgomery’s life and ministry. Like that volume, the Lanier lecture series brought together diverse intellectual voices united by a common conviction: Christianity deserves serious consideration, and its truth claims can be examined with both intellectual honesty and spiritual conviction.

In many respects, Lanier’s annual lecture series serves as a living Festschrift to Montgomery. Rather than simply preserving his writings and personal artifacts, it extends his influence through fresh conversations, new scholarship, and the continued defense of the Christian faith.

And there is something particularly fitting about this approach. Montgomery was never content to leave Christianity confined to private devotion or theological abstraction. He believed the Christian faith belonged in the public square, where its historical foundations, philosophical coherence, and moral implications could be openly examined.

Lanier continues that tradition admirably.

Beyond the lectures themselves, the beauty of the Lanier Library grounds adds another dimension to the experience. With its magnificent architecture, carefully maintained landscape, and extraordinary literary collections, the Library and Study Center offers an environment where truth, beauty, and goodness seem naturally intertwined. It is a place that encourages visitors not merely to acquire information but to pause, reflect, converse, and contemplate the larger questions of life.

It is little wonder that I heard the Lanier Library and Study Center has recently found its way onto the “bucket lists” of places to visit in Texas. For those interested in Christian history, theology, literature, and intellectual life, it certainly deserves consideration.

As the weekend concluded, I was struck by the generosity of the Lanier staff, the quality of the presentations, and the genuine fellowship shared among scholars, students, and visitors. The gathering was more than an academic conference; it was a celebration of a living intellectual tradition.

John Warwick Montgomery devoted much of his life to demonstrating that Christianity was intellectually defensible and historically credible. Through its remarkable library, distinguished lecture series, and commitment to thoughtful Christian engagement, the Lanier Library and Study Center ensures that his work continues to inspire future generations.

And perhaps that is the finest tribute one can offer a great scholar: not simply to preserve his legacy, but to build upon it.

Montgomery’s books may rest upon the shelves, but his intellectual vision remains very much alive.

fc0c9bf49a27824e.title: N. T. Wright at Lanier Library: Into the Heart of Isaiah
fc0c9bf49a27824e.summary:
What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common?

Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright.

Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God.

In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah, Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ.

Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life.

Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation.

Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation.

Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles

Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination.

One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles.

Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs, in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island.

“I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles.

The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years.

A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world.

While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah, Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention.

“Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.”

But it was no dog.

It was a white-tailed eagle, one of the magnificent birds associated with the Scottish Highlands.

As Wright watched, the eagle rose into the air, spreading its wings and soaring away. The moment was especially striking because he had been proofreading the very passage that speaks of mounting up with wings like eagles.

The timing was remarkable.

Before Wright could retrieve his camera, the bird had disappeared. There would be no photograph to document the encounter, only the vivid memory of a fleeting moment in which Scripture and creation seemed to converge.

“I have no photographic record,” Wright acknowledged, “but I have this etched into my mind as a kind of extra gift.”

For a scholar who has devoted much of his life to exploring the relationship between Scripture, history, and the purposes of God, the experience offered a wonderfully personal illustration of Isaiah’s enduring power.

It was also a reminder that biblical imagery is not confined to the ancient world. Sometimes, the words of the prophets come alive in the ordinary—and occasionally extraordinary—moments of life.

The Enduring Light of Isaiah

Listening to Wright, I was reminded that the relationship between the Old and New Testaments is not merely one of prediction and fulfillment, but of a continuous, unfolding narrative. Isaiah supplies much of the language, imagery, and theological imagination through which the New Testament writers proclaim the significance of Jesus.

And perhaps that is what made Wright’s personal stories so compelling. Here was a distinguished biblical scholar, someone who has spent decades studying the intricacies of Scripture, still finding wonder in the words of an ancient prophet and in the sight of an eagle soaring over the Scottish countryside.

Scholarship, at its best, need not diminish wonder. It can deepen it.

The setting itself seemed particularly appropriate. Surrounded by the beauty of Lanier Library, a place dedicated to the preservation and study of Christian history, theology, and biblical scholarship, Wright’s presentation brought ancient prophetic words into contemporary conversation.

In the end, the connection between Jesus and Isaiah is not simply a matter of shared themes or fulfilled prophecies. It is the story of God’s faithfulness, from the promises spoken through a prophet centuries before Christ to their fulfillment in the person and work of Jesus.

Isaiah saw the promise on the horizon. In Jesus, Wright reminds us, that horizon began to break into history.

And perhaps, like the eagle rising over the Scottish Highlands, that promise still invites us to lift our eyes, renew our hope, and recognize that God’s purposes extend far beyond what we can presently see.

By Charles Gardner —

When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned.
Amazingly, even though he was sucked underneath the waves with others as the ship went down, torpedo officer Michiharu Shinya somehow survived this 1942 disaster. (Only 18 of the 200-strong crew did).

But he would rather have died at that point as his people had been indoctrinated to believe that it was shameful to be captured. Nevertheless, he was badly wounded but nursed back to health by medics.

In time, he was picked up and eventually taken to a Prisoner-of-War camp at Featherston, near Wellington, in New Zealand, where he was to spend the next three years, as Don Stephens records in his inspirational book War and Grace (Evangelical Press, an imprint of 10Publishing).

Shinya and his fellow inmates were treated with much kindness (in sharp contrast to the torture often experienced by Allied prisoners at the hands of the Japanese). Being showered with gifts at Christmas, a feast he knew nothing about, seemed especially strange.

However, he was determined not to be ‘taken in’ by the Christian teaching offered after some of the prisoners requested spiritual help and a Japanese Bible was made available.

That is until he chanced upon an article entitled ‘Sorrow in Victory’ in which the author quoted a ‘Hebrew prophet’ as saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They shall soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint.”

It made a deep impression on him, and he was determined to find out where it came from. Assuming it was from the Old Testament, he began reading the Bible, starting at Genesis chapter 1. Eventually, to his joy, he discovered that the profound words were from the Book of the prophet Isaiah (chapter 40, verse 31).

After flagging somewhat in his search, he found himself hospitalised with malaria when a friend brought him a booklet called The Reason Why explaining the way to salvation.

It so happened that the camp’s chaplain, Pastor Hessell Troughton, had been a missionary to Japan and spoke the language. Shinya joined others in his Bible studies and came to know and love Jesus as his Saviour. So much did this “complete freedom” now rule his life that prison had morphed into what he described as “a unique paradise on earth”.

He never looked back after that and became convinced that his post-war calling would be in service of his Lord.

When he finally returned home, his family were shocked to see him alive for he had been reported as killed in action. He had also given a false name to his captors because of the supposed shame of falling into enemy hands.

Shinya subsequently became a pastor and prolific writer and translator following years of theological study both in Tokyo and the US.

The Old Testament, he came to believe, demonstrated that sin is “the ultimate problem of mankind” and clearly pointed to Christ as the answer.

On seeking to understand why so few Japanese became Christians, he felt it was partly due to their pride borne of believing they were a superior race.

As for those three Christmases he spent in New Zealand, author Don Stephens writes: “Of all the gifts he received, the one he valued most was ‘the boundless and deep grace and peace of God in the Lord Jesus Christ’.”

d51943c7dd26b8f2.title: In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words
d51943c7dd26b8f2.summary:
With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star, the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott.

Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of one of America’s most celebrated novelists. Having written about McMurtry’s faith—or lack thereof—in a previous article, following an earlier visit to Archer City, I’m returning with a somewhat different interest. This time, my attention turns to Grover Lewis, the gifted journalist, critic, and poet whose life intersected with McMurtry’s during their college years.

Lewis’ story, however, begins not with literary achievement but with almost unimaginable tragedy. As a child, he experienced the devastating loss of both parents when his father murdered his mother and was subsequently shot with the same gun, either by his dying wife or another person present.

Lewis was only eight years old.

It is difficult to imagine a more horrific beginning. Yet rather than allowing that tragedy to become the entirety of his story, Lewis eventually found a voice through literature. Perhaps the cards life dealt him gave him plenty to write about. Or perhaps writing became his way of making sense of a world that had revealed its cruelty far too early.

In his autobiographical poem “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes:

“You asked me once, Ann/Over coffee gone cold with talk/In your mother’s rain-drowsy/House, who they were, how it/Was with them in their breathless/Time in the wilds of years.”

For Lewis, those early years were indeed wild. But they were also the soil from which his literary imagination would eventually grow.

A Life in Words

Born in Texas in 1934, Grover Lewis emerged as a distinctive voice in American journalism, particularly through his cultural criticism and reporting on the rapidly changing landscape of the 1960s and 1970s.

He became known for his sharp observations, literary flair, and ability to capture the personalities and contradictions of American culture, even if he occasionally stretched the truth in the telling. His work appeared in prominent publications, including Rolling Stone, where his reporting helped establish his reputation as an insightful, sometimes cutting observer of popular culture.

Lewis was more than a journalist, however. He was a poet and literary craftsman, someone who understood that words could do more than convey information. They could illuminate the human condition, expose its contradictions, and perhaps even provide a measure of healing.

Continuing “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis ponders:

“At last, breathless and dry-mouthed/With private desire in the blue,/Swollen dark, we all lie down together—/My mother, my father, their perishing/Dreams, and I this unborn prisoner son…”

There is something haunting about these lines. The dead remain present. The past refuses to disappear. And the poet, even as an adult, seems to wrestle with the circumstances that shaped his entrance into the world.

Yet the very act of writing suggests something else: a refusal to remain silent.

Two Texans, Two Literary Paths

Lewis and Larry McMurtry crossed paths as students at North Texas State College, now the University of North Texas, during the 1950s. Both were young Texans drawn to literature and the possibilities of the written word.

Their friendship developed within a shared intellectual environment, one that encouraged reading, conversation, and the pursuit of literary ambitions.

Although their careers eventually followed different paths—McMurtry toward novels, screenplays, and literary fame, Lewis toward journalism, poetry, and cultural criticism—they shared an interest in the complexities of American life.

Both possessed an ability to look beyond the mythology of Texas and the American West, recognizing the loneliness, contradictions, and brokenness beneath its expansive skies.

McMurtry gave us cowboys, dreamers, wanderers, and lonely souls struggling against the passing of an era. Lewis offered another kind of portrait: the restless, sometimes wounded American searching for identity amid the upheavals of modern culture.

Neither writer was particularly interested in sentimentalizing Texas. They understood that beneath the romance of open ranges, dusty streets, and Western independence lived ordinary people carrying extraordinary burdens.

In different ways, both became chroniclers of a changing America. And both understood that stories, even painful ones, deserved to be told.

When Tragedy Becomes Testimony

What interests me most about Lewis is not simply that he endured an appalling childhood tragedy, but that he transformed his experiences into a life devoted to observation, reflection, and artistic expression.

Tragedy does not automatically produce wisdom, nor does suffering guarantee greatness. Some wounds remain painfully unresolved. Indeed, Lewis’ own writing suggests that the ghosts of his childhood never entirely departed.

Yet his life reminds us that the opening chapter of one’s story need not determine its conclusion.

Through writing, Lewis found a means of confronting the world rather than retreating from it. His accomplishments did not erase the suffering of his childhood, but they demonstrated that beauty, insight, and meaning can emerge even from deeply fractured beginnings.

In this respect, Lewis’ life reminds me somewhat of Esther.

The Bible tells us that Esther lost both parents, though the circumstances of their deaths remain unknown. Raised by her cousin Mordecai, she eventually became queen and intervened courageously on behalf of her people.

Her early loss did not prevent her from becoming an instrument of deliverance.

Lewis, of course, never rose to political office, perhaps a blessing for both him and the politicians he might have encountered. But he, too, refused to let tragedy become his only identity. Instead, he turned his pain toward the pen.

And, in his own way, he helped elevate his people—Texans—giving them a voice, holding up a mirror to their triumphs and tragedies, their peculiarities and passions.

Though Lewis spent much of his adult life away from Texas, a Texan he remained.

There is a distinction worth making here. Neither Esther’s story nor Lewis’ suggests that suffering is somehow necessary for a meaningful life. Evil does not become good simply because something worthwhile follows it. Rather, their stories remind us that human beings possess a remarkable capacity to respond to loss with courage, creativity, and purpose.

From a Christian perspective, this is one of the quiet mysteries of providence: not that God authors evil, but that evil need not have the final word.

The Stories We Carry

As we make our way toward Archer City, I find myself thinking about these two writers whose lives briefly converged in a Texas college town, passing the region where McMurtry’s first novel-to-screen took place, Hud. Starring Paul Newman, the movie the film put McMurtry on the map.

Prior to the trip, I read Lewis’ account of the filming of the Oscar-winning The Last Picture Show and his small but intriguing role in McMurtry’s larger story. In Western Star, biographer David Streitfeld unpacks some of the truths and fables surrounding their friendship. No, they did not witness Elvis Presley being beaten up, despite the colorful mythology.

But perhaps that is fitting. Writers, after all, inhabit that curious territory between memory and imagination, fact and interpretation, experience and invention. Both Lewis and McMurtry understood the power of stories, and both left behind words that continue to invite readers into their worlds.

Perhaps that is one of literature’s greatest gifts: it allows us to see beyond the circumstances of a person’s life and into the depths of the human spirit.

For Grover Lewis, the story began in darkness. Yet even when tragedy writes the opening lines, it need not hold the pen for the rest of the story.

Near the conclusion of “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes:

“Yet still a sealed autumn’s eternity/Locked away in the globey mound/Somewhere between their/Heaving, coupled, lonely skins.”

The imagery is unsettling, almost claustrophobic. His parents remain bound together in memory, their lives and deaths inseparable from his own existence.

Lewis’ life was intricately bound and wound in the deaths of his parents. In a theological sense, perhaps ours are as well, bound to our first, frail parents, Adam and Eve, whose disobedience introduced the fracture that runs through the human story.

We inherit a world of beauty and brokenness, promise and pain. We are born into stories we did not choose, shaped by circumstances we cannot control, and left to wrestle with questions that seldom yield easy answers.

Yet the Christian story does not end with Adam and Eve. It moves from the garden of human failure toward another garden, where an empty tomb announces that death and despair do not possess ultimate authority.

That, too, is a story of darkness giving way to light.

Beneath the Western Stars

As I settle into our room at the historic Spur Hotel in Archer City, I read from Lewis that the building served as production headquarters during the filming of The Last Picture Show. It seems a fitting place to reflect on McMurtry, Lewis, and the peculiar endurance of words.

Outside, Archer City remains a quiet Texas town, its streets and buildings bearing witness to lives that have come and gone. The Western landscape stretches beyond it, indifferent, perhaps, to the literary legends it helped produce.

I think about McMurtry’s fictional characters, so often caught between longing and disappointment, and about Lewis, whose childhood was shattered before he had scarcely begun to understand it.

Neither man’s life offers a simple lesson. Literature rarely does. Their stories contain contradictions, disappointments, achievements, and unresolved sorrows. They remind us that human lives are seldom as orderly as the narratives we construct around them.

And yet, something endures.

McMurtry’s novels remain on bookshelves. Lewis’ writings continue to speak across the decades. Their words outlast the circumstances that produced them, carrying fragments of human experience into the lives of readers they would never meet.

Perhaps this is the quiet triumph of words. They cannot undo a murder, restore a childhood, or return the dead to life. They cannot erase every regret or mend every fractured relationship.

But they can bear witness. They can preserve memory. They can help us recognize beauty where we least expect it and discover companionship in another person’s sorrow.

And sometimes, they can offer hope.

As evening settles over Archer City, I find myself grateful for these two Texans and the stories they left behind. Their lives remind me that while we cannot always choose the opening chapters of our existence, we may still participate in writing what follows.

For Lewis, the darkness of childhood never entirely disappeared. But neither did it extinguish his creative light.

We need not romanticize suffering to recognize the possibility of redemption. Nor must we pretend that every wound heals completely in this life. Some sorrows remain, even as we learn to live, love, and create alongside them.

And perhaps the greatest encouragement is this: our beginnings may shape us, but they need not imprison us.

Beneath the wide Texas sky, I am reminded that the same stars shine over lives both broken and beautiful. The night may be long. The road may be uncertain. But there is still light enough to travel by. And there are still stories worth telling.

8aefdf2b867f6ad3.title: Jewish army doctor turned to Jesus after witnessing patient’s courage

By Charles Gardner —

A Jewish army surgeon was amazed by the courage of a young soldier badly wounded in the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War (1861-65).

Dr Max Rossvally was forced to amputate both a leg and arm in a bid to save the boy’s life.

But it changed his own life. For the 17-year-old Drummer Boy – too young for frontline duty – refused chloroform or brandy to dull the pain.

Charlie Coulson chose instead to trust in Jesus, his Lord and Saviour. The doctor – an army major and Orthodox Jew – was understandably stunned by the boy’s bravery, as well as his boldness in declaring his faith in Christ and imploring the officer (whom he knew to be Jewish) to put his own trust in Jesus, since he was also the Jewish Messiah.

Max, however, was shaken rigid, and in a great dilemma, as he had always been taught to hate Jesus. For his people had largely rejected him as an ‘impostor’ and false Messiah.

Charlie died just days later, apparently more concerned for the doctor’s eternal destiny than for his own painful exit from this life.

Ten years later, Max found himself in a barber’s chair in New York once more being urged to trust in Jesus. Having explained the gospel, the barber promised to pray for him and said that, whenever he came in contact with a Jew, he felt it his duty to introduce him to the one who came for “the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6).

The surgeon subsequently boarded a train for a business meeting in Washington, where a newspaper advertisement drew him to a ‘revival’ service where the preacher echoed the messages he had heard from the barber and the boy soldier, leaving him in tears.

He agonised at home in prayer for some time afterwards, struggling most of all with the thought that, if he accepted Christ, he would be going against all the advice and teaching he had known, not to mention the Jewish community as a whole.

But he finally became convinced that Jesus was indeed the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecies (in particular, Genesis 49:10, Micah 5:2 and Isaiah 7:14).

So he prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You know I am sincere in this thing. If Jesus Christ is the Son of God, reveal him to me this night, and I will accept him as my Messiah.”

A long battle ensued, but his doubts were eventually replaced by joy and happiness as he praised God that he had found the true Shiloh, Ruler of Israel and Emmanuel.

He was to pay a high price, however, as do all who follow Christ. His wife walked out on him; his parents disowned him. But he never gave up hope as he constantly prayed and reached out to his family. After 54 days, his wife joined him as a disciple of Jesus and, in time, his daughter also became a believer. But his son disowned him for many years until he was eventually reconciled both with his earthly and heavenly Father.

In an extraordinary sequel some 18 months after he came to Christ, Max met up with Mrs Coulson, the mother of his dying young patient all those years earlier on the battlefield. With great joy, he was able to share how her son had set him on the path to a glorious future in Christ, which was to touch lives across the world, including my home county of Yorkshire in England. In fact, he came to live in Leeds to reach out to the Jewish community there and is buried at Lawnswood Cemetery in the city.

An Irish friend of mine, Colin Nevin, has visited the grave, which includes an excerpt from one of the doctor’s hymns, I am Coming Soon, and was able to give a copy of Max’s story to a caretaker, so continuing the evangelist’s legacy more than a century after his death in 1892, aged 64.

A 54-minute movie – Rossvally: From the Synagogue to the Saviour – has been produced on DVD and can apparently be ordered online.

d7345c6e16296019.title: Churches meet urgent needs as funding shortages limit Sudan relief

Sudan (MNN) — Severe funding shortages mean that aid groups can help only one in ten people in Sudan, home to the world’s largest humanitarian crisis. Nearly 20 million Sudanese face acute hunger, including five million at emergency levels.

Denis* is a ministry representative partnering with churches in Sudan. He says significant challenges remain, and conditions on the ground are growing increasingly desperate.

“A lot of health infrastructure, clinics, have either been uprooted or destroyed because of war, and that is putting a lot of pressure on women and children.

“A number of children are malnourished. Food will continue to be the greatest need.”

(Representative AI photo created with ChatGPT)

Even if returning Sudanese farmers had everything needed to plant next year’s crops, Denis adds, “There is also inadequate rainfall, so the expectation is that the need for food will be even greater in subsequent years.”

War deepens hunger and disease risks

Sudan’s crisis is driven by a war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces that began in April 2023, forcing millions from their homes and disrupting farming, trade, and livelihoods.

“The Sudan situation remains the largest humanitarian crisis because there are so many people who have been forcefully displaced,” Denis says.

Fighting and restrictions on aid prevent food and medicine from reaching vulnerable communities, while severe drought and rising prices make food harder to grow or afford. Damaged health services and shortages of clean water leave hungry families more vulnerable to disease.

“Hygiene facilities are not sufficient to provide the needed resources to the people, and that poses a risk of cholera and other communicable diseases,” Denis explains.

“This conflict has to come to an end; there have to be intentional ways and means of engaging in conversation that will lead to peace. It’s not going to be easy, but it’s a route that has to be taken,” he continues.

“Without that, fighting is not going to stop, and the problems that we have here are going to continue for a very, very long time.”

Local churches pair help and hope

Denis and his organization help local churches respond to their communities’ greatest needs by pairing practical aid with the Gospel.

AI-generated illustration of a Sudanese volunteer sharing food with a displaced family.

“Sometimes, when we look at the Gospel, we think it’s proclamation. The Gospel is a combination of proclamation and demonstration of the love of Christ,” Denis says.

In Sudan, he continues, “Demonstration is much, much more needed than proclamation, because people’s immediate needs are food, health and nutrition, trauma healing. We need to act on those things.”

This approach often leads to life-changing conversations. “When believers respond to needs in the way that Jesus would have responded, people begin asking questions: ‘Why are you doing this?’” Denis says.

“And that is what opens up opportunity to speak about the love of Christ.”

Pray for food and relief to reach families facing hunger. Pray that Sudanese will turn to Christ as they encounter the hope only He can offer.

“At Keys for Kids Ministries, we use digital technology. We use it every day. It’s like going into the mission field, right? You go, and you talk to the people that you’re trying to reach the way they want to be reached. Right now, that’s where kids are today.”

Pakistan (MNN) — Reports indicate a significant decline in registered blasphemy cases in Pakistan.

While the development offers some hope for the country’s Christian minority, concerns remain over vigilante violence and the unpredictable enforcement of blasphemy laws.

Greg Kelley with Unknown Nations comments on the reported decline.

“We’re always going to welcome reduction in these blasphemy cases, which quite honestly were just out of control, even a couple years ago.”

However, fewer blasphemy cases do not necessarily mean greater safety for Christians. “It doesn’t necessarily mean that Christians are safe because the laws remain on the books,” Kelley explains.

He points to another concern: the vigilante violence surrounding blasphemy accusations.

“It’s the vigilante justice that’s attached to that.”

In predominantly Muslim Pakistan, many incidents of persecution against Christians never reach the public eye.

“There’s a lot of reports and cases that don’t even make the media that are going on because it’s embedded in the culture, the anti-Christian sentiment.”

Yet blasphemy laws remain a serious threat to Christians due to their unpredictable and often severe application.

“The trick is all the interpretation of it, and a lot of times it’s biased.”

Lasting change will require more than a decline in registered cases. It will take a cultural shift toward religious freedom and respect for individual beliefs.

“People should have the right to decide who are they going to worship.”

Despite the challenges, Unknown Nations and its local partners continue serving communities in Pakistan.

“Jesus has called us to go into these very difficult places. And so the way we do it at Unknown Nations is through a network of indigenous leaders that have been vetted.”

USA (MNN) — Court orders have temporarily protected some Afghans from deportation, but the fate of Afghan refugees in the United States remains uncertain.

Judges temporarily blocked some individual deportations amid reports of plans to remove about 150 Afghan nationals from the U.S. Advocates began raising alarms at the end of October when documents revealed administration plans to deport Afghans as part of a wider crackdown on illegal immigration.

Lawyers and advocacy groups warn that the current push could set a dangerous precedent for future transfers. Activists say Afghans forced to return – especially those who helped U.S. forces – could face torture or worse.

“Every person’s situation is different, but some people may face serious risk because of their past work, personal history, or beliefs,” FMI’s Nehemiah says.

“In Afghan political conditions, the Taliban consider everyone to be a spy who works with the U.S. government or the Western world, so the minimum punishment is death.”

Afghan allies’ hopes for safety face new uncertainty

As the Taliban returned to power in the summer of 2021, Afghan Christians faced intensified threats; militants even had a “hit list” of known believers. Thousands of Afghan citizens were evacuated and came to the U.S. after the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Kabul.

A U.S. Marine hands out boxes of snacks to refugee children and families at Hamid Karzai International Airport, August 2021. Care packages with diapers, baby wipes, formula, and snacks were sent to the troops to help with refugee aid. (U.S. Air Force photo)

More than 40 percent of Afghans who have arrived as a part of Operation Allies Welcome are eligible for Special Immigrant Visas (SIVs) because they took significant risks to support our military and civilian personnel in Afghanistan, employed by or on behalf of the U.S. government in Afghanistan or our coalition forces, or are a family member of someone who did.

“A large number of Afghan nationals who came to the U.S. in 2021 or after that, many of them have placed their faith in Christ,” Nehemiah says.

90623669584cb433.title: Sweeping Anti-Conversion Law Leads Indian Churches to Cancel Vacation Bible Schools
90623669584cb433.summary:
Churches in the Indian state of Maharashtra are reportedly cancelling Bible camps during Diwali, a Hindu holiday celebrated during the autumn season, because of a recently enacted anti-conversion law.

For context, Maharashtra is India’s second most-populous state and includes Mumbai, the largest city in the country. Only about 2.3% of India’s 28 million people identify as Christians, making believers an extreme minority in the nation.

Much like in the U.S., the Bible camps — vacation Bible schools — last several days and consist of music, games and competitions, and stories and lessons based on Scripture, all for children ranging in ages from five to 15 years old. In India, they typically take place in the fall, according to Premier Christian News.

Some area churches, though, have cancelled their planned VBS events altogether, while others have restricted it strictly to Christian kids — a shift from the typical strategy of using the Bible camps as opportunities to evangelize.

It all comes down to Maharashtra’s sweeping Freedom of Religion Act, signed into law by Indian President Droupadi Murmu on July 30 and enacted the following month. The language of the bill is so broad, critics are concerned it will result in the penalization of Christians and churches. The law states violators may face up to seven years in prison for the non-bailable offense.

The new law bans conversion by “allurement,” a vague and overly generalized term that includes “any temptation in the form of … any gift, gratification, easy money or material benefit either in cash or kind.” It also disallows the offer of employment, “free education in school or college run by any religious body or institution,” a “better lifestyle,” “portraying practice, rituals and ceremonies or, any integral part of a religion in a detrimental way vis-a-vis another religion,” or even “glorifying one religion” — in this case, Christianity — over another.

Additionally, anyone who intends to convert from one religion to another is required to give notice to a governmental authority 60 days prior “to such proposed conversion.” At that point, the official will announce the impending conversion to the involved parties, “calling for objections within [30] days from issuance of notice,” according to the law.

“If any objections are received or otherwise, the competent authority [government official] may make an enquiry through police with regard to the intention, purpose or cause of the proposed conversion,” the bill states, noting that, if a violation is suspected, an investigation will ensue.

According to Premier, at least 12 other states in India have similar anti-conversion laws and, while advocates argue the bills protect vulnerable people from exploitation, others see them as a clear attack on Christian evangelism. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, for example, has said the laws disproportionately affect Christians and Muslims, and have noted terms like “allurement” are intentionally ambiguous and problematic.

The churches moving ahead with planned VBS initiatives are requiring registration and charging entree fees of 50 to 100 rupees (roughly $1) as a way to prove parents sent their children to these faith-based camps intentionally and of their own accord.

03de9fd7be4edf75.title: Evangelist Claims Police Threatened to Arrest Him For Preaching Jesus at Christmas Festival

Evangelist David Hoffman is pushing back after he says police demanded he go to a “remote speech zone” while sharing the Gospel during a holiday festival last year in Tucson, Arizona.

First Liberty, a First Amendment legal advocacy firm, is taking on his case and pushing back against what it calls “open hostility to religious speech” that is “blatantly unconstitutional.”

Attorney Garrett Bell sent a demand letter asking the city to step back, arguing that what happened at the Winterhaven Festival of Lights was improper.

“I run an outreach and evangelism ministry called Kingdom Enterprises,” Hoffman told CBN News. “We do U.S.-based street ministry and evangelism. We’re based in Tucson, Arizona, and … there’s a winter event that we have traditionally gone to pretty much every year over the past 10 years — except for COVID — and we go, and we have conversations with people.”

The team hands out Gospel tracts and shares about Jesus. He said this became a problem in 2025, when they went to the event, and police officers approached them before they were fully set up.

“Police approached us, and they told us that, if we continued within the event, we would be ticketed and arrested,” Hoffman said.

Hoffman recalled asking the police questions and said cops affirmed they had the authority to arrest him, which left him concerned about continuing to push back. So, he listened to the authorities and went to the free speech zone. Then, he later reached out to First Liberty.

Bell said this alleged interaction amounted to censorship, adding that the push to send people to supposed “free speech zones” is deeply problematic.

“We like to just call it a ‘designated speech area,’ because there’s nothing free about it,” Bell said. “They’re largely unconstitutional.”

Bell said it was also troubling that Hoffman had been to the event many times before without incident, and added that this was the first year festival organizers received a permit from the city of Tucson that included this free speech policy — one purportedly dictating that there could be “no religious messaging or materials distributed.”

“You have to be in this designated speech area, and that area is outside of the main footprint of the event,” Bell said. “And it’s sort of this small, confined, barricaded space where Hoffman and his group were pretty well separated from anyone they really wanted to reach.”

The entire ordeal left Hoffman shocked, because he said the event is public. In his view, the suggestion he and his group should be disallowed is wrong.

Bell filed a complaint and a motion for preliminary injunction, but the first step they took was to send a demand letter to the city.

“To this day, they [have] not responded [to our letter] and, because the Winterhaven Festival is right around the corner for 2026, we filed that complaint and preliminary injunction,” Hoffman said. “And, as of now, have not received an answer or response from the city.”

CBN News will continue to cover the story as it unfolds. A request for comment from the city has not been returned.

511bb82e05f84568.title: Are Demons Real? New Data Reveals Americans’ Experience With Spiritual Attacks
511bb82e05f84568.summary:
Spiritual warfare is a real part of the human experience, and the Bible explicitly details how events in the spiritual realm affect people.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms,” Ephesians 6:12 (NIV) reads, with verse 13 continuing: “Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand.”

The question isn’t if people will experience spiritual warfare; it’s when. A new survey from the American Bible Society (ABS) explores what Americans believe about spiritual warfare, specifically measuring how many people believe they have faced such attacks (watch CBN’s documentary “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons” today).

Dr. John Plake, editor-in-chief of the State of the Bible series and chief innovation officer at ABS, told CBN News that around 1-in-4 Americans report facing spiritual warfare.

“We saw real difference here across levels of faith participation,” he said. “About a fourth — 26% — of American adults say they’ve had that experience.”

He continued, “[Fifty-eight percent] of practicing Christians would agree with that statement, casual Christians, 28%, nominal Christians, 24%, and then non-Christians, 10%.”

The topic itself is quite fascinating, as Plake said it’s sometimes hard to quantify what a spiritual attack denotes. And since there’s not “a lot of deep data” there’s not qualitative information to help understand what respondents believe a spiritual attack looked like or entailed.

“I’m sure these people do have stories that they can tell about times when they felt like the negative experiences that they were having couldn’t be attributed just to natural causes, that there was some form of spiritual opposition that was going on,” Plake said. “And to see that incidence be that high, I was pretty fascinated by it.”

Another factor ABS was able to screen for was people’s reaction to a perceived spiritual attack — and those statistics were equally interesting.

“So 74% of people who [said they faced attack] said that the way they respond to spiritual attack is that they pray,” Plake said. “I think that makes a lot of sense, right? When spiritual attacks come, you may not be in a particular context where it’s easy to do much else, but you can always pray.”

The second-highest percentage was 36%, who said they declare Christ’s authority.

“There is this kind of sense that … they’re aware they’re in a spiritual battle, that their opposition isn’t … the person who may be opposing them at the moment,” Plake said. “But actually, there’s a spiritual thing going on here, and so they declare Christ’s authority.”

Next came the 24% who said they listen to praise and worship music, but then there’s the smallest — and most concerning — percentage: the 15% who said that they meditate on or quote Scripture.

“I would have hoped that would be a little bit higher,” Plake said. “And I think it also presents an opportunity for pastors and church leaders to recognize, ‘Hey, there are a lot of people, particularly in the church, who are having these experiences, and how can we equip them biblically to respond when they’re facing these kinds of spiritual attacks or moments of opposition, or even when there’s a need for a miraculous healing?'”

For more on this topic, watch “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons.”

Episode 400 – How Chick-fil-A Plans to Feed the Future | David Farmer

Host Justin Forman sits down with David Farmer, Vice President of Innovation and New Ventures at Chick-fil-A. Together they look at how a company grows for 80 years without losing the things that make it what it is. The first Chick-fil-A restaurant opened in 1967. It was about 350 square feet inside an Atlanta mall, with room for roughly six seats. Today some Chick-fil-A operators move 500 cars through a single drive-through, which means a customer leaves with food every seven and a half seconds.

WATCH | LISTEN

EPISODE NOTES

The first Chick-fil-A fit about six seats inside an Atlanta mall. Today, some operators move 500 cars an hour through one drive-through. David Farmer, Vice President of Innovation and New Ventures at Chick-fil-A, sits down with Justin Forman to explain how that happened without losing the personal, caring service people expect.

David traces Chick-fil-A’s innovation back to founder Truett Cathy. Truett deboned a chicken breast to turn tables faster, pioneered food in the mall, and built an operator model with a $10,000 refundable deposit and a 50/50 profit split. From there, the conversation covers Dan Cathy’s rogue lemonade recipe, the bottleneck that led to one juicing facility in California, the race from 100 cars an hour to 500, and the three-legged stool every new idea has to stand on.

For founders trying to grow without drifting, David offers a simple principle: get clear on what cannot change, then play freely inside the fence line. Watch the full episode on YouTube or continue to stream audio on your favorite podcast platform.

By Charles Gardner —

A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there.

And he was led to the conclusion that everything he has been taught to believe about the Jews is a lie.

Luai Ahmed was invited to address the assembly by UN Watch, a non-governmental organisation monitoring the international body’s performance, as the UN Human Rights Council gathered to debate racism.

He said: “I grew up in Yemen, where the word that we used for black people is ‘abeed’, which quite literally means ‘slaves’. Racism towards black people in my country is horrifying, but it’s not even the most toxic hatred that I was taught.

“The first time I ever heard the word ‘Jew’ was in my local mosque when I was nine years old. At the end of Friday prayers, the Imam said: ‘May Allah kill the Jews and the Zionists’. And I responded alongside thousands of Muslims praying beside me: ‘Ameen’.”

Luai then continued: “I was taught that Zionism meant killing Arabs, stealing our land, and destroying Islam. Then October 7th came. Hamas terrorists ‘freed Palestine’ by slaughtering 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping more than 200 people, including a one-year-old child.

“Almost everyone in my Arab-Muslim circle celebrated. I didn’t. Instead, as a journalist, I decided to visit the so-called Zionist entity, and I was completely shocked to the core by the lack of apartheid and racism that I experienced.

“One day, I got an eye infection. At the hospital, the nurses in reception were Jewish. The doctor treating me was Arab. Is there racism in Israel? Of course. There’s racism everywhere.

“But Arabs in Israel aren’t called ‘slaves’. They are doctors, engineers, and party leaders. My experience helped me realise that Zionism really just means the Jewish people’s right to a tiny country. Everything I was taught was a lie.”

Quite apart from tipping over the tables of woke left-wing ideology spreading its poisonous antisemitic tentacles across the globe, Luai’s testimony also knocks holes into the escalating pressure on the UK to make reparations for the slave trade, which saw plenty of collaborators in the host countries of those who suffered. And of course, the truth that dare not speak its name – that it was Christians like William Wilberforce who put an end to it!

Luai is a great inspiration to fellow journalists like me who long for more of our colleagues to stand up and be counted.

 

Thanks also to David Soakell of Christian Friends of Israel’s Watching Over Zion newsletter, November 5, 2026.

7d8f851d84600d22.summary:
Paraguay (MNN) — The fallout continues from the November 3 collapse of digital bank Ueno in Paraguay, which has shaken the country’s trust in leaders.  

Ueno’s questionable loan practices have had consequences outside of its leadership team. Within the week, Congress impeached and arrested President Santiago Peña for his ties to the bank. 

Peña was initially charged with “breach of trust and administration for personal gain” but now faces criminal charges as well. (More on that here.) Eight Ueno executives and three former central bank officials have also been arrested.

Maralina Alfonso is TWR’s marketing and communication director for Latin America and the Caribbean. She lives in Paraguay. 

“We are feeling a grief, a pain because the country was with much hope and was happy,  because our ex-president is a man who has a nice family. He grew up with [a] mother and father. His family are workers and smart people, and he used to go to Catholic church,” says Alfonso. 

“We are disappointed, you know. We are like, ‘a lie, everything was lie.’”

The collapse of Ueno Bank unsurprisingly resulted in its customers losing access to their accounts. According to Ueno, it had 2.9 million customers, but the Central Bank says Ueno had 1.8 million depositors. In a country of around 7.1 million people, both numbers are still a large portion of the population. 

Alfonso says that each day they hear of more investigations being opened into the bank scandal. But to her, what is deeply concerning is that bank leadership included people with a Christian background. 

“Many of them, many of those brilliant millennials, grew up in a Christian school. So the question is, what happened?” she says. “How the greed and the love [of] the money bury the Word of the Lord in those hearts?”

Asunción, Paraguay (Stock photo courtesy of Unsplash)

Alfonso says people are angry with the ex-president’s family, and the families of those involved in Ueno Bank’s mismanagement, even those who had nothing to do with the scandal. This could put them in physical danger. 

“My country is a small country, and Asunción is very small. You go to the supermarket, you know everybody,” she says. “They cannot go to the shopping, to a restaurant, anywhere. [Pray] the Lord with a miracle will restore those people, name and family and relatives. [It] is terrible.”

RTM Paraguay is TWR’s local partner. Their team shares biblical radio programs in Spanish and Guarani. Pray that their programs will speak wisely to the concerns of these days and point people to God. 

“RTM Paraguay has their own professional expertise producing content in [the] Guarani language. Those programs are broadcast on 42 radio stations, especially in the countryside, in the rural area,” says Alfonso.

Here are ways Alfonso asks for prayers for Paraguay at this time:

  1. For those waiting for their money: retirees, pension holders, depositors above the guaranteed limit, and small businesses, that the Lord would provide and sustain them.
  2. For officials: wisdom for President Pedro Alliana, and integrity for prosecutors and judges (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
  3. For justice with truth: transparency, restitution, and no revenge.
  4. For peace: that violence and chaos would not take hold.
  5. For the Church: humility, protection from attacks, and pastors who speak without fear about greed (2 Timothy 4:2).
  6. For hearts: repentance and reconciliation, and that this pain would open doors to the gospel.

ee6fa0e6954c3539.title: “The Issachar Question” and what it means for us
ee6fa0e6954c3539.summary:
Sudan (MNN) – Among David’s mighty men of Israel were those from the tribe of Issachar. 1 Chronicles 12:32 describes these men as people who understood the times and advised Israel according to their wise discernment. 

Dr. Yassir Eric draws from this passage what he calls, “The Issachar Question.” 

“Wherever we are as Christians, we should always ask God, ‘What are you doing?’” Eric says. 

His ministry, Ekkios, aims to provide a church home for Muslim‑background believers around the world. Eric himself is a former Muslim from Northern Sudan, where war and famine have ravaged his people for decades. In the midst of heartbreaking realities with devastating consequences, he asks the Issachar question: Lord, how are you at work?

“And the Lord is doing so many things. In the midst of this destruction, in the midst of the suffering, people are coming to know the Lord,” he says.

In 1995, when Eric left Sudan, he knew a single Christian in the Islamic region of Darfur. Today, the situation is brighter. 

“There are hundreds of thousands of people from Darfur who are coming to know the Lord – in the refugee camps, those who are in Iran – the Lord is meeting them in the midst of this hardship,” he says.

It is Christ who orients, gives hope, and unifies people in the midst of divisive times. 

“No political system brought us together, but Jesus,” Eric states.

He believes that civically informed, spirit-led Christians are uniquely poised to shape society. 

“We need to understand what God is doing,” Eric says. “We need to understand what we have to do to be part of this whole story – what I call the story of God.” 

As you both trust and trace the Lord’s hand in current events, Eric encourages you to remember your root system: the gospel of Jesus Christ. And like the men of Issachar, would you ask the Lord to help you rightly discern these times?

df5c9fa5b210fba1.title: World Missionary Press Scripture booklets empower outreach in Africa
df5c9fa5b210fba1.summary:
Africa (MNN) — God’s Word can change lives and transform hearts. That’s why World Missionary Press partners with local Christians and groups like Every Home for Christ to get Scripture into the hands of as many people as they can.

(Graphic courtesy WMP)

During a recent missions’ convention in Johannesburg, South Africa, “We were able to take some of our new literature, and they loved it. We came back with requests for one of our new pieces, The Power of Hope, to be in Kiswahili, and in Afrikaans, and some languages of Nigeria,” WMP’s Helen Williams says.

“These are just fun times because they’re times of sharing, and rejoicing about what the Lord is doing; the relationships are deepened every year.”

Additionally, Gospel workers are ready for WMP Scripture booklets in four new locations: Comoros, Djibouti, Eritrea, and Sudan. Each location presents its own difficulties, from spiritual oppression in Comoros to civil war in Sudan. Yet hope is coming.

“It’s hard [soil] for the Gospel,” Williams says.

“[These are] places that we had hoped to get material in whenever the Lord opened the door, and now Every Home for Christ has been able to establish a director in those countries.”

Empowered for ministry

Hearts change when people read God’s Word in their language. The Lord also uses the distribution process to grow believers’ faith. Take one distributor in Equatorial Guinea, for example.

“I met him two years ago in Ethiopia; he came over to me at breakfast, and he said, ‘I’m going to need some literature!’” Williams recalls.

(Photo courtesy of WMP)

Since WMP already had an established distribution partner in Equatorial Guinea, Williams suggested the young man should begin by connecting with that partner to learn more.

“I gave him the name, and he just lit up like a Christmas tree. He said, ‘Oh, I know him! He’s one of my friends. Okay, I’ll talk to him,’” Williams says.

“So, in the course of the last two years, he’s been getting material from our coordinator in Equatorial Guinea. Then, he decided that he needed his own shipment.”

The young man was shocked to learn that WMP would send free booklets to support his outreach vision.

“He said, ‘I was going to ask you for more material, and then I got the word that the shipment came, and some of it’s for me,’” Williams shares.

“‘Now I’ve got the tools. Now I can do what the Lord’s given me to do. Thank you, thank you, thank you!’”

By giving online, you can help WMP print and send Scripture booklets to Gospel workers like this one.

“We trust that the Lord’s going to touch hearts and do His work through His Church, through His people, His way,” Williams says.

“It’s always exciting to talk about what the Lord’s doing, and look forward to what He will do, and to lean on Him when we don’t know what to do.”

The reason the Vine and its branches are such a true parable of the Christian life is that all nature has one source and breathes one spirit. The plant world was created to be to man an object lesson teaching him his entire dependence upon God, and his security in that dependence. He that clothes the lilies will much more cloth us. He that gives the trees and the vines their beauty and their fruits, making each what He meant it to be, will much more certainly make us what He would have us to be. The only difference is what God works in the trees is by a power of which they are not conscious. He wants to work in us with our consent. This is the nobility of man, that he has a will that can cooperate with God in understanding and approving and accepting what He offers to do.
If ye abide--Here is the difference between the branch of the natural and the branch of the spiritual Vine. The former abides by force of nature: the latter abides, not by force of will, but by a divine power given to the consent of the will. Such is the wonderful provision God has made that, what the power of nature does in the one case, the power of grace will do in the other. The branch can abide in the Vine.
If ye abide in me...ask whatsoever ye will--If we are to live a true prayer life, with the love and the power and the experience of prayer marking it, there must be no question about the abiding. And if we abide, there need be no question about the liberty of asking what we will, and the certainty of its being done. There is the one condition: "If ye abide in me." There must be no hesitation about the possibility or the certainty of it. We must gaze on that little branch and its wonderful power of bearing such beautiful fruit until we truly learn to abide.
And what is its secret? Be wholly occupied with Jesus. Sink the roots of your being in faith and love and obedience deep down into Him. Come away out of every other place to abide here. Give up everything for the inconceivable privilege of being a branch on earth of the glorified Son of God in Heaven. Let Christ be first. Let Christ be all. Do not be occupied with the abiding--be occupied with Christ! He will hold you, He will keep you abiding in Him. He will abide in you.
If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you--This He gives as the equivalent of the other expression: "I in you. If my words abide in you"--that is, not only in meditation, in memory, in love, in faith--all these words enter into your will, your being, and constitute your life--if they transform your character into their own likeness, and you become and are what they speak and mean--ask what ye will; it shall be done unto you. Your words to God in prayer will be the fruit of Christ and His words living in you.
Ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you--Believe in the truth of this promise. Set yourself to be an intercessor for men; a fruit-bearing intercessor, ever calling down more blessing. Such faith and prayer will help you wonderfully to abide wholly and unceasingly.
If ye abide. Yes, Lord, the power to pray and the power to prevail must depend on this abiding in Thee. As Thou art the Vine, Thou art the divine Intercessor, who breathest Thy spirit in us. Oh, for grace to abide simply and wholly in Thee, and ask great things!

Andrew Murray, The True Vine (1898), day 16 of 31. Public domain. Source

feed.title: 🌿 The True Vine · Day 1: The Vine
feed.html:
I am the True Vine--John 15:1


All earthly things are the shadows of heavenly realities--the expression, in created, visible forms, of the invisible glory of God. The Life and the Truth are in Heaven; on earth we have figures and shadows of the heavenly truths. When Jesus says: "I am the true Vine," He tells us that all the vines of earth are pictures and emblems of Himself. He is the divine reality, of which they are the created expression. They all point to Him, and preach Him, and reveal Him. If you would know Jesus, study the vine.
How many eyes have gazed on and admired a great vine with its beautiful fruit. Come and gaze on the heavenly Vine till your eye turns from all else to admire Him. How many, in a sunny clime, sit and rest under the shadow of a vine. Come and be still under the shadow of the true Vine, and rest under it from the heat of the day. What countless numbers rejoice in the fruit of the vine! Come, and take, and eat of the heavenly fruit of the true Vine, and let your soul say: "I sat under His shadow with great delight, and His fruit was sweet to my taste."
I am the true Vine.--This is a heavenly mystery. The earthly vine can teach you much about this Vine of Heaven. Many interesting and beautiful points of comparison suggest themselves, and help us to get conceptions of what Christ meant. But such thoughts do not teach us to know what the heavenly Vine really is, in its cooling shade, and its life-giving fruit. The experience of this is part of the hidden mystery, which none but Jesus Himself, by His Holy Spirit, can unfold and impart.
I am the true Vine.--The vine is the living Lord, who Himself speaks, and gives, and works all that He has for us. If you would know the meaning and power of that word, do not think to find it by thought or study; these may help to show you what you must get from Him to awaken desire and hope and prayer, but they cannot show you the Vine. Jesus alone can reveal Himself. He gives His Holy Spirit to open the eyes to gaze upon Himself, to open the heart to receive Himself. He must Himself speak the word to you and me.
I am the true Vine.--And what am I to do, if I want the mystery, in all its heavenly beauty and blessing, opened up to me? With what you already know of the parable, bow down and be still, worship and wait, until the divine Word enters your heart, and you feel His holy presence with you, and in you. The overshadowing of His holy love will give you the perfect calm and rest of knowing that the Vine will do all.
I am the true Vine.--He who speaks is God, in His infinite power able to enter into us. He is man, one with us. He is the crucified One, who won a perfect righteousness and a divine life for us through His death. He is the glorified One, who from the throne gives His Spirit to make His presence real and true. He speaks--oh, listen, not to His words only, but to Himself, as He whispers secretly day by day: "I am the true Vine! All that the Vine can ever be to its branch, "I will be to you."
Holy Lord Jesus, the heavenly Vine of God's own planting, I beseech Thee, reveal Thyself to my soul. Let the Holy Spirit, not only in thought, but in experience, give me to know all that Thou, the Son of God, art to me as the true Vine.

Andrew Murray, The True Vine (1898), day 1 of 31. Public domain. Source
